pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Rhizoctonia disease of potato are caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn (teleomorph Thanatephorus cucumeris [A. B. Frank] Donk)

type_of_disease.quote: is caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani Kühn

affected_parts.quote: The symptoms of the disease are found on both above- and below-ground portions of the plant.

summary.value: Black scurf appears as irregular, black to brown hard masses (sclerotia) on the tuber surface; underground sprouts, stems, and stolons develop brown cankers/lesions that may be superficial or large, sunken, and necrotic; reddish to dark brown girdling cankers form on stems at or below ground; a delicate white mycelial mat may form on stems just above the soil line; aerial tubers and leaf curl may also occur.
summary.quote: The irregular, black to brown hard masses on the surface of the tuber are sclerotia, or resting bodies, of the fungus (Figure 1).

diagnostic_features.value: Black sclerotia (scurf) adhere tightly to the tuber skin but are superficial and do not penetrate or damage the tuber interior ('the dirt that doesn't wash off'); Rhizoctonia lesions are always dry and usually sunken, distinguishing them from wet rots; reddish to dark brown girdling cankers on stems at or below ground are also characteristic.
diagnostic_features.quote: These sclerotia are often referred to as black scurf and give rise to the name

value: Seed tuber decay caused by Fusarium species or soft rot bacteria
look_alikes.quote: Poor stands may also be mistaken for seed tuber decay caused by Fusarium or soft rot bacteria unless plants are dug up and examined ... Poor stands and stunted plants can also be caused by blackleg, a bacterial disease ... A leaf curl, which can be confused with symptoms of the potato leaf roll virus, has also been reported in severely infected plants.

affected_parts.quote: Plants with blackleg are stunted and have a stiff, erect growth habit. Foliage becomes chlorotic and the leaflets tend to roll upward at the margins. Plants generally are wilted. Stems of infected plants exhibit an inky black decay.

summary.value: Plants are stunted with a stiff, erect growth habit, chlorotic foliage with leaflets rolling upward at the margins, general wilting, and stems showing an inky black decay often rotting the stem base completely; initiates from the seed tuber and progresses up the stems causing a wet, sometimes slimy rot.
summary.quote: Plants with blackleg are stunted and have a stiff, erect growth habit. Foliage becomes chlorotic and the leaflets tend to roll upward at the margins. Plants generally are wilted. Stems of infected plants exhibit an inky black decay . The base of the stem is often completely rotted.

diagnostic_features.value: The characteristic inky black stem decay; in relatively dry soil only the pith may show blackening; produces a wet, sometimes slimy rot in contrast to Rhizoctonia lesions which are always dry and usually sunken.
diagnostic_features.quote: Stems of infected plants exhibit an inky black decay . The base of the stem is often completely rotted. In relatively dry soil, only the pith may show blackening.

look_alikes.quote: The soft rot Pectobacterium spp. may cause wilting but affected plants lack the characteristic inky black stem decay.

conflicts.note: Cornell and MSU extension sources mention blackleg as a look-alike but do not name the pathogen; UC IPM provides the specific pathogen name Pectobacterium atrosepticum.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Streptomyces scabies causes common scab of potato.

type_of_disease.quote: Common scab of potato, which has a worldwide distribution, is caused by filamentous bacteria in the genus Streptomyces .

affected_parts.quote: Infections can also occur on the stems, stolons, or roots.

summary.value: There are no aboveground symptoms. On actively growing tubers, small (5–8 mm) circular tan to brown rough-textured spots appear that may merge into irregular patches. Lesions on tubers are variable, generally appearing as rough, corky lesions ranging from small and raised to deeply pitted. Brown to tan oval to round spots may also be seen on stems and stolons.
summary.quote: There are no aboveground symptoms. ... When tubers are actively growing, small (5-8 mm) circular spots appear on the tubers. These spots may grow together to make irregularly shaped patches. Spots are usually tan to brown in color and are rough in texture.

diagnostic_features.value: Infections begin as small tan to reddish-brown spots on the tuber surface; roughness may be flat (russet scab), raised (raised scab), or sunken/pitted (pitted scab, dark brown to almost black); pitted scab can penetrate up to one-half inch into the tuber; flesh underneath the spot is straw colored and somewhat translucent when sliced.
diagnostic_features.quote: The roughness may be flat to the tuber (russet scab) or raised up (raised scab). The rough area may be sunken into the tuber (pitted scab), and usually dark brown to almost black in color. ... If the tuber is sliced open, the flesh underneath the spot is straw colored and somewhat translucent.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Fusarium sambucinum is considered the most aggressive pathogen for this disease in major parts of Europe, China and North America (Secor and Salas 2001 ; Du et al. 2012 ).

type_of_disease.quote: However, dry rot is a fungal disease where a pattern of shrinking, shriveling and non-slimy lesion development is observed on the surface of tubers (Fiers et al. 2012 ).

affected_parts.quote: The tubers and roots are the main plant parts that are directly affected by dry rot disease.

summary.value: External symptoms first appear as non-descript flecks that expand to wrinkled dark brown to black lesions; internally, hollow cavities of dry rotted brown-to-gray tissue develop, often with tufts of white or variously colored fungal growth. Advanced disease results in mummified tubers.
summary.quote: On the tuber surface, external symptoms may first appear as non-descript flecks and expand to wrinkled lesions that may appear dark brown to black (Figure 1). Internally, hollow cavities with dry rotted tissue of various shades of brown to gray develop within tuber tissue, with tufts of fungal growth of white or various colors often visible within cavities and associated with lesions on the tuber surface (Figure 2).

diagnostic_features.value: Dry (not wet/slimy) internal brown-to-gray rot forming hollow cavities with tufts of white, yellow, pink, or variously colored fungal growth within cavities; external sunken dark area; shrinking and shriveling non-slimy lesions distinguish it from bacterial soft rot, and unlike late blight it penetrates into the center of the tuber.
diagnostic_features.quote: Extensive rotting causes the tissue to shrink and collapse, usually leaving a dark sunken area on the outside of the tuber (Figure 2) and internal cavities (Figure 3). Yellow, white, or pink mold may be present (Figure 4).

look_alikes.quote: Several other diseases and physiological disorders , including Pythium leak, pink rot, late blight, and suboxygenation (blackheart), also cause brown to black internal discoloration of tubers.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Early blight is a common fungal disease of solanaceous crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplants) caused by Alternaria solani .

type_of_disease.quote: Early blight is a common fungal disease of solanaceous crops

affected_parts.quote: The disease affects leaves, stems, and tubers, and can reduce tuber yield and size.

summary.value: Symptoms first appear as circular dark-brown spots on leaves and stems that can later develop concentric, target-like rings, often surrounded by yellow margins. Lesions are sometimes limited by veins, giving an 'angular' appearance. Early foliar symptoms often appear near the base of the plant, spreading up to higher leaves as the disease progresses. On tubers, lesions appear as dark, sunken, cork-like spots with raised margins.
summary.quote: Symptoms first appear as circular dark-brown spots on leaves and stems that can later develop concentric, target-like rings, often surrounded by yellow margins. Lesions are sometimes limited by veins, giving an \

diagnostic_features.value: Early blight foliar lesions can be diagnosed in the field by the characteristic dark concentric rings alternating with bands of light-tan tissue, giving them a distinctive target spot appearance. This feature is absent in brown spot and black dot lesions. Lowest, oldest leaves are infected first; tuber lesions are sunken, circular, with a well-defined margin and underlying brown, corky, dry rot more than 0.12 inch deep.
diagnostic_features.quote: Early blight foliar lesions can be diagnosed in the field by the characteristic dark concentric rings alternating with bands of light-tan tissue, giving them a distinctive target spot appearance (Figure 1a).

value: Brown spot (caused by small-spore Alternaria species)
look_alikes.quote: Initial early blight lesions may be confused with brown spot (caused by small-spore Alternaria species) (Figure 2a) or black dot (caused by Colletotrichum coccodes) lesions (Figure 2b).

conflicts.note: NDSU explicitly states tubers are also affected; UW-Madison and PNW Handbooks focus on leaves and stems but also note tuber lesions. Canonical value reflects the most commonly cited parts; tubers are noted in the diagnostic features.

type_of_disease.quote: Potato pink rot is a water mold or oomycete disease of potato tubers

affected_parts.quote: Wilting starts from the base of the stem and progresses upward, causing leaf yellowing, drying and defoliation. Vascular discoloration and blackening of the underground stems may also be observed. Similarly, roots may turn brown to black

summary.value: The soilborne pathogen causes darkened, water-soaked lesions with defined margins near the stem-end of the tuber, and is often identified by the characteristic pink/salmon color and ammonia-like odor of a potato cut and exposed to air after 20-30 minutes. Potato vines can also appear stunted or wilted later in the season, with noticeable leaf yellowing and drying as the wilt moves up the stem.
summary.quote: The soilborne pathogen causes darkened, water-soaked lesions with defined margins near the stem-end of the tuber, and is often identified by the characteristic pink/salmon color and ammonia-like odor of a potato cut and exposed to air after 20-30 minutes. Potato vines can also appear stunted or wilted later in the season, with noticeable leaf yellowing and drying as the wilt moves up the stem.

diagnostic_features.value: As tubers are exposed to air, the infected tissue progressively changes from cream to salmon pink within 15 to 30 minutes (then brown, then black after about an hour); the tough, leathery, rubberlike texture of infected tubers with an ammonia-like odor distinguishes pink rot from bacterial soft rot.
diagnostic_features.quote: The tough, leathery, rubberlike texture of infected tubers distinguishes pink rot from bacterial rot disease in which the diseased tissue becomes soft and pulpy and contains numerous cavities.

value: Bacterial soft rot / rot caused by Pectobacterium spp.
look_alikes.quote: The tough, leathery, rubberlike texture of infected tubers distinguishes pink rot from bacterial rot disease in which the diseased tissue becomes soft and pulpy and contains numerous cavities. However, infected tissues are easily invaded by secondary pathogens, such as soft rot bacteria (Pectobacterium spp.)

conflicts.note: MSU Extension pink rot page did not explicitly state the disease type; UW Vegetable Pathology explicitly identifies it as oomycete/water mold.
MSU states 15-30 minutes for cream-to-pink color change; UW states 20-30 minutes. Both are consistent in range; UW value used as canonical.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: P. carotovorum subsp. carotovorum (syn. E. c . subsp. carotovora ) is associated with aerial stem rot, lenticel rot, and soft rot

type_of_disease.quote: Potato soft rot is caused by the bacterium Pectobacterium carotovorum

affected_parts.quote: Soft rot symptoms on the foliage include weak, chlorotic (yellowed) plants with margins of leaflets curled upwards. Stem lesions are usually light brown but can be colorless, but not black. Stems will rot and become very mushy.

summary.value: On tubers, soft rot first appears as small, tannish, water-soaked spots that rapidly enlarge into a soft, blister-like decomposed area, often with slimy/watery ooze; rot is white to cream-colored, turning brown to black after air exposure with a sharp delineation between infected and healthy tissues, becoming a foul-smelling mass. Foliage shows weak, chlorotic plants with leaflet margins curled upward.
summary.quote: Soft rot on tubers first appears as small, tannish, water-soaked spots on the surface. These spots rapidly enlarge and the tissue decomposes in a soft, blister-like area on the surface of the tuber. Often, a slimy or watery substance oozes from breaks in the blister.

diagnostic_features.value: Tuber tissues become soft, wet, rotted, cream to tan in color; upon exposure to air tissues may turn brown to black creating a delineation between infected and healthy tissues; stem lesions are light brown or colorless but not black; stems become very mushy; rot is relatively odor free though secondary organisms usually cause a foul smell.
diagnostic_features.quote: Tuber tissues becomes soft, wet, rotted and are cream to tan in color. Upon exposure to air, tissues may turn brown to black in color around the infected areas, creating a delineation between infected and healthy tissues. Although rot of the soft-rot bacterium is relatively odor free, secondary organisms usually cause a foul smell.

look_alikes.quote: Blackleg and bacterial soft rot are diseases that are caused by different, but closely related bacteria.

conflicts.note: University of Maine uses the species-level name Pectobacterium carotovorum without subspecies designation; PNW Handbooks specifies subsp. carotovorum, which is the more precise current usage.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Sclerotium rolfsii Sacc. (Athelia rolfsii (Curzi) Tu & Kimbrough) is a necrotrophic, soilborne, fungal plant pathogen

type_of_disease.quote: is a necrotrophic, soilborne, fungal plant pathogen that is present in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide

affected_parts.quote: Stem lesions expand up and down the stem, and all plant parts can be infected. Stem infection leads to wilting and yellowing of the foliage.

summary.value: Affected stems show a moist decay at or slightly below the soil surface; lesions expand up and down the stem causing wilting and yellowing of foliage. Infected plants show pale green leaves that cluster and cup upwards followed by whole-plant wilting and decaying outer crown tissue. White radiating mycelium covers infected plant parts and nearby soil; white-to-tan sclerotia mature to dark brown. In potato tubers, small round sunken lesions with brownish margins appear on lenticels, later becoming deeply sunken and yellow or tan.
summary.quote: typically, plants with early infections have pale green leaves that cluster and cup upwards. Eventually the whole plant wilts. ... Close inspection of affected plants reveals decaying outer tissue at the crown of the plant ... Often a white mat of mycelium is observed at the base of the stem at the soil line ... small, spherical, white to tan structures with a smooth, hard texture, known as sclerotia, are observed. The sclerotia turn yellow and subsequently dark brown as they mature. ... In potato tubers, for example, small, round, sunken lesions with a brownish margin appear on lenticels. Later the lesions become deeply sunken and turn yellow or tan.

diagnostic_features.value: Presence of white radiating mycelium and brown sclerotia (0.5–2 mm in diameter) at the base of the stem at the soil line; sclerotia are small and spherical, white when young and brown when mature. Tubers may show cheesy moist decay with sclerotia bursting out of rotten tissue.
diagnostic_features.quote: later symptoms are easily distinguished from symptoms of these diseases by the presence of white mycelium and brown sclerotia at the base of the stem

look_alikes.quote: Field distribution occurs in a patchy pattern, which could be confused with symptoms of other soilborne diseases, such as Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt , or bacterial wilt

conflicts.note: UC IPM uses 'Sclerotium Stem Rot'; INRA ephytia uses 'Stem rot or Southern blight'; Virginia Tech uses 'Southern blight'. All refer to the same disease caused by Sclerotium rolfsii.
INRA ephytia only mentions stem bases and tubers; UC IPM and VT extension describe broader plant involvement including foliage and whole plant wilting.

conflicts.canonical_value: White mat of mycelium and brown sclerotia at the base of the stem; sclerotia 0.5–2 mm, white when young, brown when mature
conflicts.alternative_value: Spectacular symptoms of numerous sclerotia bursting out of rotten tubers, with fan-like mycelium on stem bases
conflicts.note: INRA ephytia emphasizes post-harvest tuber symptoms with sclerotia bursting out of rotten tubers as a key diagnostic feature.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Tomato spotted wilt is caused by Tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV), which is closely related to Impatiens necrotic spot virus (INSV)

type_of_disease.quote: Tomato spotted wilt is a common viral disease of worldwide distribution

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of TSWV range from chlorosis, mottling, stunting and wilting to severe necrosis of leaf, stem and fruit tissues.

summary.value: On potato, TSWV causes leaf spots with a target appearance (similar to early blight but smaller and clustered); clustering of spots can leave large completely dark brown to black areas, often at the leaf base; stems and petioles show dark brown areas and growing points can be killed; leaves may also develop yellow, brown or black ringspots (sometimes target-like) and necrotic areas with or without yellow haloes; on tubers, TSWV causes deformation, splits, cracks, dark spots and concentric brown necrotic arcs with internal necrosis and rot.
summary.quote: A characteristic symptom of TSWV infecting potato is leaf spots with a target appearance similar to early blight, but the spots are smaller and tend to be clustered. Clustering of spots can result in affected leaves having large areas that are completely dark brown to black, more often at the leaf base. Stems and petioles often have dark brown areas. Growing points can be killed.

diagnostic_features.value: Leaf spots have a target appearance like early blight but are smaller and tend to be clustered; clustering produces large dark brown to black areas often at the leaf base; unlike fungal diseases, there are typically symptomless plants next to affected plants; black streaks on petioles/stems with branch tip dieback; on tubers, external or internal concentric brown necrotic arcs.
diagnostic_features.quote: the spots are smaller and tend to be clustered. Clustering of spots can result in affected leaves having large areas that are completely dark brown to black, more often at the leaf base... unlike fungal diseases such as early blight, typically there are plants with no symptoms next to affected plants.

look_alikes.quote: On potato leaves, tomato spotted wilt can lead to necrotic (i.e., dead) areas with or without yellow haloes. These symptoms can resemble symptoms of early blight.

conflicts.note: Wisconsin Extension and Cornell Extension list only Foliar and Stem; the French seed potato source additionally mentions root/tuber tissues via 'fruit tissues' and tuber symptoms, supporting inclusion of Root/Tuber.
